displayQuestion: Why modernization has no single answer

blocks.text: As railways, schools, factories, banks and modern governments became more widespread, societies appeared to use similar tools. Yet relationships among states, capital and society did not become identical. Modernization did not end divergence; it changed the level at which differences were organized.

Societies had to connect new capabilities to their own histories. Land, class, religion, language and colonial experience did not vanish when new institutions appeared. Inherited conditions could provide resources or impose limits, shaping how reform unfolded.

The central questions became who controlled the state, owned capital, participated in politics and bore the costs of development and empire. Modern capabilities could serve different power structures. Factories, railways and schools alone did not establish a common outcome.

Modernity is therefore better understood as capabilities that spread and recombine than as one destination every society must reach. Similar pressures could generate different paths. Volume V carries this question toward the next volume: how would the encounter among these different modern societies reorganize the world again?
